39: This buddhi has been explained to you as sāṅkhya gives it. Now hear it as yoga gives it. Yoked with this buddhi, son of Pṛthā, you will cast off the bondage of action.
40: Here nothing that is begun is lost, and there is no setback. Even a very little of this dharma protects one from great fear.
41: Here, joy of the Kurus, the buddhi that is resolute by nature is one. For the buddhis of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
42: There is this flowery speech that the undiscerning proclaim, son of Pṛthā. They delight in the words of the Vedas and say that there is nothing else.
43: Desire is their nature, and heaven is the highest thing they know. What that speech gives is birth, as the fruit of action, and it is full of particular rites aimed at attaining enjoyment and lordship.
44: In those who cling to enjoyment and lordship, whose thought has been carried away by that speech, the buddhi that is resolute by nature is not established in samādhi.
45: The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain. Be free of the three guṇas, Arjuna: free of the pairs of opposites, always standing in sattva, free of gaining and keeping, in possession of the self.
46: For a brahmin who knows, there is as much use in all the Vedas as there is in a well when water is flooding on every side.
47: Your rightful claim is to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and do not let yourself be attached to inaction.
48: Do your actions established in yoga, Dhanañjaya, giving up attachment and staying even in success and failure. Evenness is what is called yoga.
49: For action is far lower than the yoga of buddhi, winner of wealth. Seek refuge in buddhi. Those whose motive is the fruit are pitiable.
50: One who is yoked with buddhi casts off both good deeds and bad deeds here. So yoke yourself to yoga. Yoga is skill in actions.
51: For the wise, yoked with buddhi, give up the fruit that is born of action. Freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the state where there is no affliction.
52: When your buddhi crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, you will become indifferent to what is yet to be heard and to what has been heard.
53: When your buddhi, perplexed by what is heard, stands unmoving and unshaken in samādhi, then you will attain yoga.
54: How is one whose wisdom is steady to be described, Keśava, one who stands in samādhi? How would a person whose thought is steady speak, how would they sit, how would they walk?
55: When a person casts off all the desires that have entered the mind, son of Pṛthā, and is content in the self alone, by the self, then that person is called one whose wisdom is steady.
56: One whose mind is not shaken in sorrows, who no longer craves pleasures, and whom passion, fear and anger have left, is called a sage of steady understanding.
57: One who is without fondness anywhere, who meets with this or that, pleasant or unpleasant, and neither rejoices nor hates: that person's wisdom is firmly established.
58: And when such a one draws the senses completely in from the objects of the senses, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, that person's wisdom is firmly established.
59: The objects turn away from the embodied one who takes no food, but the taste does not. Once that one has seen the supreme, even the taste turns away.
60: For the churning senses, son of Kuntī, carry off the mind by force, even the mind of a discerning person who strives.
61: Restraining them all, one should sit yoked, holding me as the highest. For when a person's senses are under control, that person's wisdom is firmly established.
62: When a person dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment to them arises. From attachment desire is born, and from desire anger arises.
63: From anger comes delusion, and from delusion, confusion of memory. From the loss of memory comes the ruin of buddhi, and from the ruin of buddhi one is lost.
64: But one whose self is governed, who moves among objects with senses that are freed from passion and aversion and under the control of the self, attains clearness.
65: In that clearness, all of that person's sorrows come to an end. For when the mind is clear, buddhi quickly becomes steady.
66: One who is not yoked has no buddhi, and one who is not yoked has no contemplation. One who does not contemplate has no peace. And where would happiness come from for one who has no peace?
67: For when the mind is led along after the roaming senses, it carries away a person's understanding, as the wind carries away a boat on the water.
68: Therefore, mighty-armed one, when a person's senses are held back on all sides from the objects of the senses, that person's understanding is firmly established.
69: In what is night for all beings, the self-restrained one is awake. What beings are awake in is night for the sage who sees.
70: The waters enter the ocean, which keeps being filled yet rests on an unmoving foundation. In the same way, the one whom all desires enter reaches peace, and not the one who desires desires.
71: The person who gives up all desires and moves about without longing, without the sense of mine, without the sense of I, attains peace.
72: This is the standing in brahman, son of Pṛthā. One who has reached it is not deluded. One who stands in it, even at the time of the end, reaches the nirvāṇa of brahman.
